headline: Bushu, “radical”, is from Middle Chinese 部首, first mentioned in Chinese in the Shūowén Jiězì of roughly 100 CE.

sources.quote: From Middle Chinese 部首 (MC buX syuwX). First mentioned in Chinese in the Shūowén Jiězì of roughly 100 CE.

headline: Arai is cognate with 粗い (arai).

sources.quote: Cognate with 粗(あら)い (arai).

meaning: to expand, to swell (out), to become inflated
headline: Fukuramu, “to swell”, is 膨 (fukura, “a bulge, a swelling”) plus -mu, first cited to the mid-800s.

sources.quote: First cited to the mid-800s.

From 膨, 脹 (fukura, “a bulge, a swelling”) + む (-mu, suffix indicating “looks like, seems like”). The fukura portion is in turn from now-archaic verb 膨る, 脹る (fukuru, “to swell, to bulge”), superseded by modern 膨れる, 脹れる (fukureru) of the same meaning.

headline: Massaki is 真っ (ma'-, “truly”) plus 先 (saki, “first”).

sources.quote: From 真っ (ma'-, “truly”) + 先 (saki, “first”).

headline: Ji, “character”, is from Middle Chinese 字.

sources.quote: From Middle Chinese 字 (MC dziH).

meaning: to avoid (physical contact); to ward off, to avert
headline: Sakeru is from 避く (saku), cognate with 裂ける (sakeru).

sources.quote: From 避(さ)く (saku), cognate with Japanese 裂ける (sakeru). See the page for 避(さ)く (saku) for more information.

headline: Kō, “this way”, shifted from 斯く (kaku): kaku, kau, kɔː, then kō.

sources.quote: /kaku/ → /kau/ → /kɔː/ → /koː/
Shift from 斯(か)く (kaku).

headline: Aruiwa is ある (aru, “to be, to exist”) plus a nominalizing い plus は (wa, topic marker), and arose from 漢文訓読.

sources.quote: ある (aru, “to be, to exist”, 連体形 (rentaikei) of the classical verb あり (ari)) + い (i, nominalizing suffix) + は (wa, topic marker). Arose from 漢文訓読 (kanbun kundoku).

meaning: to breathe in, to suck; to smoke
headline: Suu, “to suck”, is likely an onomatopoeia; the page compares words from Middle Korean to Proto-Indo-European.

sources.quote: From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *supu. Cognate with Okinawan 吸ぷゆん (shipuyun).
Likely an onomatopoeia. Compare Middle Korean ᄲᆞᆯ〮다〮 (spóltá, “to suck”), Middle Chinese 吸 (MC xip, “to suck”), Proto-Austronesian *-sep (“to suck”), Proto-Indo-European *sewg- (“to suck”), etc.

headline: Senshū, “last week”, is first attested in the 1920s.

sources.quote: First attested in 1920s.

headline: Tomaru, “to stay overnight”, is a doublet of 止まる (tomaru).

sources.quote: Doublet of 止(と)まる (tomaru).

headline: Kai, “shell”, was kapi in Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *kapi.

sources.quote: ⟨kapi₁⟩ → */kapʲi/ → /kaɸi/ → /kawi/ → /kai/
From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *kapi. Appears voiced in the Kojiki of 712 CE in a compound, with the phonetic man'yōgana spelling 賀比, and in the Man'yōshū, completed some time after 759 CE.

meaning: to take up, to pick up; to confiscate
headline: Toriageru is 取る (toru, “to take”) plus 上げる (ageru, “to raise, lift”).

sources.quote: 取(と)る (toru, “to take”) + 上(あ)げる (ageru, “to raise, lift”)

headline: Doku, “poison”, is from Middle Chinese 毒.

sources.quote: From Middle Chinese 毒 (MC dowk).

headline: Minna is a shift from みな (mina), with a doubled consonant added.

sources.quote: Shift from みな (mina), adding gemination.

headline: Kitai is Sinitic 氣體 (qìtǐ).

sources.quote: Sinitic 氣體 /气体 (qìtǐ)

headline: Jinsei is from Middle Chinese 人生.

sources.quote: From Middle Chinese 人生 (ȵiɪn ʃˠæŋ).

headline: Junjo is 順 (jun, “order”) plus 序 (jo, “order”): “order” twice.

sources.quote: From 順 (jun, “order”) + 序 (jo, “order”).

headline: Nemuru shifted from neburu, from the same root as Old Japanese 寝 (nu), which gives 寝る (neru).

sources.quote: Shift from ねぶる (neburu), from the same root with Old Japanese 寝 (nu) (whence 寝る (neru, “to sleep; to lie down”)), in turn from Proto-Japonic *naynpuru. Cognate with Kunigami 眠ん (ninbin /⁠níɴbîɴ⁠/), Northern Amami Ōshima 眠るり (nïbururi), Okinawan 眠じゅん (ninjun /⁠níɴdʑùɴ⁠/), Okinoerabu 眠ゆん (nibuyun /⁠nìbújúɴ⁠/), Southern Amami Ōshima 眠っゆむっ (nïpyum /⁠nɨ́pjùm̩⁠/), 眠りゅむっ (nïpryum /⁠nɨ́pɾʲùm̩⁠/), Tokunoshima 眠びゅい (ninbyui /⁠nɪ́ɴbʲúɪ́⁠/), Yoron 眠ゆん (nibuyun /⁠nìbùjùɴ⁠/), Miyako 眠ゔっ (niv), Yaeyama 眠ん (ninbun /⁠níbùɴ⁠/), and Yonaguni 眠どぅん (nindun /⁠níɴdúɴ⁠/).
Compare 眠い (nemui, “sleepy”), 眠たい (nemutai, “sleepy”), and おねむ (o-nemu, “(childish) sleepiness, sleep”).

meaning: to order, to command, to appoint
headline: Meijiru shifted from 命ずる (meizuru), as an s-irregular verb ending in -uru became an upper monograde verb in -iru.

sources.quote: Shift from verb 命ずる (meizuru), by natural progression from サ行変格活用 (sa-gyō henkaku katsuyō, “s-irregular conjugation”) verbs ending in -uru to 上一段活用 (kami ichidan katsuyō, “upper monograde conjugation”) verbs ending in -iru.

pos: nouns which may take the genitive case particle 'no'
headline: Hontō first appears in a text of 1770, and the clipped honto first appears in 1886.

sources.quote: First appears in the late Edo period in a text from 1770. The clipped reading ほんと (honto) with the shorter second vowel is regarded as a simple shift from original reading ほんとう (hontō), and this first appears in a text from 1886.

headline: Shiokarai is 塩 (shio, “salt”) plus 辛い (karai, “harsh (of flavor); spicy, salty”).

sources.quote: 塩(しお) (shio, “salt”) + 辛(から)い (karai, “harsh (of flavor); spicy, salty”)

meaning: to get tired of, to lose interest in
headline: Akiru comes from earlier 飽く (aku), irregularly evolved to the kami ichidan conjugation.

sources.quote: From earlier 飽(あ)く (aku), irregularly evolved to kami ichidan conjugation.

headline: Kazoeru began as kazu apu, and took six steps to reach kazoeru.

sources.quote: /kazu apu/ → /kazo₁pu/ → /kazoɸu/ → /kazwoɸuru/ → /kazo(w)uru/ → /kazoweru/ → /kazoeru/
Inherited from Old Japanese.
Development

Natural progression from Old and Classical Japanese 下(しも)二(に)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo nidan katsuyō, “lower bigrade conjugation”) verbs ending in -u to modern Japanese 下(しも)一(いち)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo ichidan katsuyō, “lower monograde conjugation”) verbs ending in -eru. For the Old / Classical form, see the 数ふ entry.

Equivalent to 数(かず) (kazu, “number”) + あう (au, “to join”). The earliest attestation of this verb uses the 下(しも)二(に)段(だん) (shimonidan, “lower bigrade”) conjugation pattern, suggesting an irregular shift from the 四(よ)段(だん) (yodan, “quadrigrade”) conjugation pattern of compounded verb あふ (afu, modern あう (au)). Compare the sporadic shift of the auxiliary verb ふ (-fu, expressing repetition or ongoing state) to える (-eru) in some terms.

headline: Shōkyokuteki is 消極 (shōkyoku) plus 的 (-teki).

sources.quote: 消極(しょうきょく) (shōkyoku) + 的(てき) (-teki)

headline: Kore is from Old Japanese; compare Okinawan くり (kuri).

sources.quote: ⟨ko₂re⟩ → /kore/
From Old Japanese. Compare Okinawan くり (kuri) and Northern Amami Ōshima くるぃ (kurï).

headline: Kuzureru comes from Old Japanese 崩る (kuduru).

sources.quote: ⟨kuduru⟩ → /kuduru/ → /kud͡zuru/ → /kud͡zureru/
From Old Japanese 崩る (kuduru), in the 下(しも)二(に)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo nidan katsuyō, “lower bigrade conjugation”) pattern.
Development

Natural progression from Old and Classical Japanese 下(しも)二(に)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo nidan katsuyō, “lower bigrade conjugation”) verbs ending in -u to modern Japanese 下(しも)一(いち)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo ichidan katsuyō, “lower monograde conjugation”) verbs ending in -eru.
First attested in the 播(はり)磨(ま)風(ふ)土(ど)記(き) (Harima Fudoki, “Harima Fudoki”) (715 CE).
Ultimately from 屑(くず) (kuzu, “rubbish, refuse, scrap, junk, waste”), and analyzable as etymologically meaning "to become rubbish". For the causative form 崩(くず)す (kuzusu), compare lay waste, ruin.

headline: Anketo is borrowed from French enquête, “inquest”.

sources.quote: Borrowed from French enquête (“inquest”).

pos: noun or participle which takes the aux. verb suru
headline: Tsure is the continuative stem of 連れる (tsureru, “to accompany, lead”).

sources.quote: From the 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 連(つ)れる (tsureru, “to accompany, lead”).

headline: Shū, “state”, is from Middle Chinese 州, and 州 is a daiyōji replacing 洲.

sources.quote: From Middle Chinese 州 (MC tsyuw).
From Middle Chinese 洲 (MC tsyuw). 州 is a daiyōji replacing 洲.
